prompt_free_text:
This paper studies a simple but important mismatch in neural theorem proving: models are typically trained only on successful proof trajectories, yet at inference time they operate inside a search process that repeatedly proposes tactics, observes failures, and backtracks. The authors propose to train on trial-and-error traces that include failed branches and backtracking decisions, and they instantiate this idea on a newly constructed Lean dataset for intuitionistic propositional logic, PropL. Empirically, they report that their model, TrialMaster, achieves higher out-of-distribution success rates and lower search cost than a conventional DFS-based prover trained only on successful proofs.

The paper has a clear motivating intuition, and I think that intuition is sound. There is indeed a train-test discrepancy in theorem proving systems that learn only from successful trajectories but are deployed inside search. The attempt to expose the model to failed branches and backtracking behavior during training is natural and worthwhile. I also appreciate that the authors build a fully formalized benchmark in Lean, where proof correctness can be checked exactly, and that they focus on a domain where complete proof-tree generation is feasible. This makes the experimental setting relatively clean.

That said, while the paper is interesting and promising, I do not think the current version fully establishes the broader claims it makes, and several aspects of the experimental design make the central conclusion harder to interpret than it should be.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the dataset construction effort. PropL appears to be a useful controlled benchmark for studying theorem proving with explicit search traces. The use of a bijection between natural numbers and formulas is an elegant way to sample formulas systematically, and the use of focused proof search to generate both successful and failed branches is well aligned with the paper’s goal. If released in a usable form, this dataset could be valuable beyond this paper. I also think the choice of intuitionistic propositional logic is defensible: it is expressive enough to require nontrivial proof search, but constrained enough that one can generate large amounts of verified data with complete search histories.

However, the paper repeatedly describes the dataset as “complete, scalable, and representative,” and these claims are overstated in the current presentation. It is not obvious that uniform sampling over formula IDs induces a meaningful or representative distribution over provable theorems of practical interest. In fact, the distribution over formulas may be heavily shaped by the encoding scheme and by conditioning on provability. Moreover, the experiments fix theorem statements to have exactly 16 internal nodes, which further narrows the distribution. The train/test split is then defined by proof-length quantiles under the authors’ own proof generator, which means “OOD” here really means longer proofs under this specific search procedure, not a broader semantic or structural shift. This is still a valid and useful evaluation protocol, but it should be described more modestly and precisely.

A central concern is that the comparison between TrialMaster and the DFS baseline is not as controlled as it needs to be. TrialMaster is not merely “the same model trained with failed traces”; it also uses a different inference interface and a different action space. It is prompted with the entire proof history including failed branches and can emit explicit backtrack instructions, whereas the DFS baseline uses a model that proposes tactics for a single state and relies on an external search controller to manage backtracking. These are substantially different systems. As a result, the observed gains cannot be attributed cleanly to “learning from failure” alone. They may also reflect advantages from richer conditioning context, a different serialization of the search state, or the ability to emit explicit control actions.

The ablation in Table 3 partially addresses this by evaluating a model trained without trial-and-error data but run in the same one-step inference style as TrialMaster. This is helpful and probably the most convincing result in the paper. Still, even here the comparison is not fully unpacked. If the model trained without trial-and-error data is asked to operate in a regime where it must implicitly manage backtracking from a history format it never saw during training, then poor performance is expected. That does support the importance of matching training to inference, but it does not isolate whether failed branches themselves are useful beyond simply teaching the model the output protocol and history format. A stronger set of ablations would separate: training on successful paths only but serialized in the same full-history format; training with backtrack tokens but without failed branches; training with failed branches but no explicit backtrack actions; and perhaps training with synthetic “do not repeat failed tactic” annotations. Without such controls, the paper’s main causal claim remains somewhat underspecified.

Relatedly, the baseline choice is weaker than it should be. The paper argues for DFS over BFS because the branching factor is small, but that does not justify excluding stronger search-based baselines more generally. Since the core claim is about leveraging failure information, the most relevant comparisons would include methods that also condition on prior failed attempts at inference time, whether through prompting, reranking, or explicit memory, even if they are not trained on full failed traces. The related work mentions COPRA and Baldur, but there is no empirical comparison, even in a simplified form. I understand that exact reproduction may be difficult in this domain, but the paper would benefit from at least a stronger discussion of why the chosen baseline is the right one for the stated claim.

Another issue is that the reported gains, while meaningful, are in a very narrow domain where the theorem space and tactic space are highly constrained and generated by the same underlying proof-search machinery used to create the data. This raises the possibility that the model is learning to imitate the idiosyncrasies of the FPS generator rather than acquiring a broadly useful notion of learning from failure. The paper acknowledges limited generality, but the conclusions sometimes read more broadly than the evidence supports. In particular, claims about “developing better tactics” should be softened unless supported by analyses showing improved tactic quality independent of the search controller and data generator.

I also found some methodological details insufficiently specified for reproducibility and interpretation. For example, the exact prompt format used for TrialMaster and the DFS tactic generator is not clearly described in the main text. Since serialization choices are likely crucial here, examples of the actual training and inference prompts are needed. The tokenization and meaning of the 1500-word limit are also unclear; elsewhere the paper refers to context length, but “word length” is not the same as token length for Llama. The stopping criteria differ between systems in ways that may matter: TrialMaster fails immediately on any Lean error, while DFS can continue exploring alternatives after invalid tactics at a state. This asymmetry could either help or hurt either side depending on the distribution of errors, and it deserves explicit discussion. Likewise, the choice to train for a single epoch with batch size 4 on over 100k theorems seems underexplained; it would be useful to know whether models were tuned to convergence, whether multiple seeds were run, and how sensitive results are to training variance.

The proof-generation procedure also introduces a notable caveat: the additional assumption that once an implication is picked, it cannot be used to show its premise makes the search incomplete, albeit rarely according to the authors. This may be acceptable pragmatically, but it means the dataset and evaluation are tied to a restricted proof-search regime. Since the paper’s thesis concerns learning from failed search paths, any heuristic restriction that changes the shape of those paths is potentially important. I would like to see more quantitative characterization of how often this heuristic changes proof structure, proof length, or branching behavior.

The empirical presentation could be improved substantially. The paper references Figure 5 for the main OOD results, but in the provided text the figure contents are not actually visible beyond a fragment. Since the OOD comparison is the core result, the paper should present a clear table with exact success rates and search costs for all key configurations, including TrialMaster, the best DFS settings, and the ablations. Confidence intervals or at least multiple random seeds would also help, especially because the reported differences among top systems are sometimes small. For example, the claimed 0.3% success-rate advantage over the best DFS configuration on 1000 test theorems corresponds to only three theorems; without variance estimates, this is hard to interpret robustly.

I did appreciate the exploratory study on proof length. The finding that shorter trial-and-error traces outperform longer ones is plausible and interesting, suggesting that not all failure information is equally useful. But the explanation remains speculative. It would be stronger to analyze what kinds of failed branches help versus hurt: repeated dead ends, shallow local alternatives, long irrelevant excursions, etc. Such analysis could turn the paper from a proof-of-concept into a more insightful study of how failure supervision should be structured.

There are also several writing and presentation issues. The paper contains many grammatical errors and awkward phrasings, and some sections are repetitive. A careful proofreading pass is needed. Some terminology is imprecise: “word length” versus token length, “complete” dataset, “representative” sampling, and “without help from an external system” even though Lean is still used to validate each tactic and compute next states. The tables also appear to have formatting issues in the provided version. These are fixable, but they currently detract from clarity.

Overall, I think the paper contains a good idea and a potentially useful benchmark, and the results are encouraging. But the current experimental evidence does not yet cleanly isolate the contribution of learning from failed search paths from other changes in system design, and the claims about representativeness and generality are stronger than warranted. I would be more enthusiastic if the paper added tighter ablations, clearer prompt/interface descriptions, stronger baselines or at least more careful justification of baseline choice, and a more modest framing of what has been demonstrated.

My main suggestions for improvement are as follows. First, add controlled ablations that disentangle failure supervision from interface changes: same history format with only successful paths, explicit backtrack tokens without failed branches, failed branches without backtrack actions, and perhaps a model that simply sees previously tried tactics at inference time. Second, report exact OOD numbers in a table, with multiple seeds if possible. Third, provide concrete prompt examples and clarify token/context accounting. Fourth, characterize the dataset more carefully: provability rate, proof-length distribution, branching statistics, and how the incompleteness heuristic affects the data. Fifth, soften claims about completeness, representativeness, and broader applicability unless additional evidence is added. Finally, if feasible, include at least one comparison to an inference-time failure-aware baseline that is not trained on failed traces, to better support the claim that training on failure itself is the key ingredient.

In summary, this is a thoughtful and potentially impactful paper in a controlled theorem-proving setting. I believe the core idea is worth exploring, and the dataset contribution may be valuable. But for a top-tier ML venue, I would want a more rigorous causal evaluation and a more careful framing before fully endorsing the paper.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies whether large language models for theorem proving benefit from training on trial-and-error trajectories rather than only successful proof paths. To enable this, the authors introduce PropL, a Lean-formalized dataset of intuitionistic propositional logic theorems with proofs generated by a focused proof search procedure that records both successful and failed/backtracked steps. They fine-tune Llama-2-7B in two settings: a conventional tactic generator trained only on correct proofs and used within a DFS search procedure, and TrialMaster, trained on proof trees with trial-and-error information and allowed to emit either tactics or explicit backtrack instructions. On their benchmark, TrialMaster reportedly achieves higher out-of-distribution success rates and lower Lean-call search cost than the DFS baseline, while both methods perform near-perfectly in-distribution.
strengths: The paper addresses a real and important mismatch in neural theorem proving: training on only successful trajectories while inference requires exploration over many failed attempts.
The proposed dataset contribution is potentially valuable: Lean formalization allows proof checking, and inclusion of trial-and-error traces is uncommon in public theorem proving datasets.
The experimental question is clear and well-motivated, and the ablation comparing training with versus without trial-and-error under a similar inference protocol is useful.
The paper evaluates both success rate and search cost, which is appropriate for theorem proving systems where efficiency matters in addition to solvability.
The setting is controlled and scientifically convenient: intuitionistic propositional logic permits reliable proof generation and verification, reducing ambiguity about correctness.
weaknesses: The empirical comparison is not fully apples-to-apples: TrialMaster and the DFS baseline differ simultaneously in training data, inference algorithm, decoding strategy, and failure handling, making causal attribution to trial-and-error learning less clean.

The benchmark domain is narrow and synthetic. Results on intuitionistic propositional logic with generated proofs may not transfer to broader theorem proving settings or human-written mathematical corpora.

The claim that PropL is 'uniformly sampled' and 'representative' is overstated. A bijection from naturals to formulas does not by itself imply a meaningful uniform distribution over formulas or theorem difficulty, especially after conditioning on provability and proof-length-based splits.
The paper provides limited statistical rigor: no variance across random seeds, no confidence intervals, and no significance testing despite relatively small test sets of 1000 examples each.

The strongest baseline appears underdeveloped. There is no comparison to stronger modern search strategies or to methods that also condition on prior failed attempts at inference time, beyond discussion in related work.

The evaluation protocol may favor TrialMaster because backtrack instructions incur no Lean calls, while DFS is charged for sampled tactic checking; this makes the search-cost metric less directly comparable across systems.

Important implementation details are missing or unclear, such as prompt formatting, exact tokenization/context accounting for the 1500-word limit, and whether theorem overlap or near-duplicate structural overlap exists across train/test splits.
methodological_flaws: The central experimental claim conflates multiple factors. TrialMaster is trained on trial-and-error traces and also uses a distinct autoregressive proof-tree generation protocol with explicit backtrack tokens and greedy decoding, whereas the baseline uses DFS with sampled tactics. Therefore the observed gains cannot be attributed solely to learning from failure.

The dataset generation/search procedure is explicitly incomplete due to the assumption that once an implication is picked, it cannot be used to show its premise. This weakens claims of completeness/representativeness of the dataset and may bias the proof distribution in ways not analyzed.

The paper's logic around 'uniform sampling' is scientifically weak. Uniformly sampling integers and mapping them bijectively to formulas does not define a natural uniform distribution over formulas unless the integer range and conditioning are carefully specified; moreover, restricting to formulas with 16 internal nodes and then filtering by proof-length quantiles further distorts the distribution.

The train/test split based on proof lengths generated by the same deterministic or near-deterministic proof procedure may induce a procedural OOD notion rather than a semantic one. The test distribution may still be highly aligned with the generator and proof-search heuristics used to create training data.

Failure criteria are asymmetric. TrialMaster fails immediately on any Lean error, while DFS can continue exploring alternative tactics after failures within a state. Conversely, TrialMaster can emit cost-free backtrack instructions. These differences complicate interpretation of both success rate and Lean-call efficiency.

The claim that the model has learned backtracking is only weakly supported: producing syntactically valid backtrack instructions that reference existing states does not establish that the model performs semantically meaningful backtracking better than simpler heuristics or templated behavior.
The paper lacks evidence that improvements are robust across seeds or model sizes. Given stochastic proof generation and fine-tuning, single-run results may overstate the effect size.

Some conclusions are stronger than warranted by the evidence, especially statements that trial-and-error training produces 'higher-quality tactics' and that the dataset is 'complete, scalable, and representative.' The experiments support usefulness in this controlled setting, but not these broader claims.
